claim: Phosphoinositides (PI) are key regulators of cellular organization in eukaryotes.
source: Phosphoinositides (PI) are key regulators of cellular organization in eukaryotes and genes that tune PI signaling are implicated in human disease mechanisms.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in cell biology supported by extensive literature.

claim: Genes that tune PI signaling are implicated in human disease mechanisms.
source: Phosphoinositides (PI) are key regulators of cellular organization in eukaryotes and genes that tune PI signaling are implicated in human disease mechanisms.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge and references throughout the manuscript.

claim: The study describes a set of CRISPR-based genome engineering tools that allow manipulation of PI signaling proteins with spatial and temporal control during metazoan development.
source: Here, we describe a set of CRISPR-based genome engineering tools that allow the manipulation of each of these proteins with spatial and temporal control during metazoan development.
evidence: The manuscript describes the generation and validation of these tools throughout the Results section.

claim: The reagents were used to deplete a set of 103 proteins individually in the Drosophila eye.
source: We demonstrate the use of these reagents to deplete a set of 103 proteins individually in the Drosophila eye and identify several new molecules that control eye development.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the Results section with experimental data and images.

claim: Several new molecules that control eye development were identified.
source: We demonstrate the use of these reagents to deplete a set of 103 proteins individually in the Drosophila eye and identify several new molecules that control eye development.
evidence: The screen results are presented in the Results section and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The head group of phosphatidylinositol can be phosphorylated combinatorially at positions 3, 4, and 5 to generate a set of seven PIs.
source: The head group of the parent lipid phosphatidylinositol can be phosphorylated combinatorially at positions 3, 4, and 5 to generate a set of seven PIs.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about PI metabolism.

claim: Phosphatidylinositol 4,5 bisphosphate [PI(4,5)P2] plays a key role in the regulation of membrane transport and the cytoskeleton.
source: These PIs are key regulators of subcellular processes; for example, phosphatidylinositol 4,5 bisphosphate [PI(4,5)P2] plays a key role in the regulation of membrane transport and the cytoskeleton (Janmey et al., 2018), whereas phosphatidylinositol three phosphate (PI3P) is an important regulator of endocytosis and autophagy (Schink et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Janmey et al., 2018.

claim: Phosphatidylinositol three phosphate (PI3P) is an important regulator of endocytosis and autophagy.
source: These PIs are key regulators of subcellular processes; for example, phosphatidylinositol 4,5 bisphosphate [PI(4,5)P2] plays a key role in the regulation of membrane transport and the cytoskeleton (Janmey et al., 2018), whereas phosphatidylinositol three phosphate (PI3P) is an important regulator of endocytosis and autophagy (Schink et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schink et al., 2016.

claim: PIs have been implicated in the regulation of nuclear function.
source: PIs have also been implicated in the regulation of nuclear function (Fiume et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fiume et al., 2015.

claim: Phosphatidylinositol 3,4,5 trisphosphate (PIP3) is an essential regulator of growth factor signaling.
source: For example, phosphatidylinositol 3,4,5 trisphosphate (PIP3) is an essential regulator of growth factor signaling and plays a conserved role in developmental control in C. elegans, Drosophila, and mammals (Engelman et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Engelman et al., 2006.

claim: PIP3 plays a conserved role in developmental control in C. elegans, Drosophila, and mammals.
source: For example, phosphatidylinositol 3,4,5 trisphosphate (PIP3) is an essential regulator of growth factor signaling and plays a conserved role in developmental control in C. elegans, Drosophila, and mammals (Engelman et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Engelman et al., 2006.

claim: Phosphatidylinositol four phosphate (PI4P) levels play a key role during cellular development in gametogenesis in Drosophila.
source: Phosphatidylinositol four phosphate (PI4P) levels play a key role during cellular development in gametogenesis in Drosophila (Brill et al., 2000; Tan et al., 2014) and a conserved role for PI(4,5)P2 is proposed in apico-basal polarity (Devergne et al., 2014; Martin-Belmonte et al., 2007; Rousso et al., 2013; Yan et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brill et al., 2000 and Tan et al., 2014.

claim: A conserved role for PI(4,5)P2 is proposed in apico-basal polarity.
source: Phosphatidylinositol four phosphate (PI4P) levels play a key role during cellular development in gametogenesis in Drosophila (Brill et al., 2000; Tan et al., 2014) and a conserved role for PI(4,5)P2 is proposed in apico-basal polarity (Devergne et al., 2014; Martin-Belmonte et al., 2007; Rousso et al., 2013; Yan et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Devergne et al., 2014; Martin-Belmonte et al., 2007; Rousso et al., 2013; Yan et al., 2011.

claim: Dysregulation in PI signaling has been linked to Lowe syndrome.
source: Dysregulation in PI signaling has also been linked to several human diseases; these include developmental disorders such as Lowe syndrome (Staiano et al., 2015) and PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum (PROS)(Madsen et al., 2018); mutations in PTEN, a key regulator of PIP3 levels are the second most frequent mutations seen in human cancers (Worby and Dixon, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Staiano et al., 2015.

claim: Dysregulation in PI signaling has been linked to PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum (PROS).
source: Dysregulation in PI signaling has also been linked to several human diseases; these include developmental disorders such as Lowe syndrome (Staiano et al., 2015) and PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum (PROS)(Madsen et al., 2018); mutations in PTEN, a key regulator of PIP3 levels are the second most frequent mutations seen in human cancers (Worby and Dixon, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Madsen et al., 2018.

claim: Mutations in PTEN are the second most frequent mutations seen in human cancers.
source: Dysregulation in PI signaling has also been linked to several human diseases; these include developmental disorders such as Lowe syndrome (Staiano et al., 2015) and PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum (PROS)(Madsen et al., 2018); mutations in PTEN, a key regulator of PIP3 levels are the second most frequent mutations seen in human cancers (Worby and Dixon, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Worby and Dixon, 2014.

claim: Mutations in genes regulating PI signaling are seen in a large number of genetic disorders of the human nervous system.
source: Mutations in genes regulating PI signaling are seen in a large number of genetic disorders of the human nervous system (Raghu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Raghu et al., 2019.

claim: The seven PIs are generated in cells by the activity of a set of evolutionarily conserved lipid kinases.
source: The seven PIs are generated in cells by the activity of a set of evolutionarily conserved lipid kinases that are specific for the substrate they will use, as well as the position on the inositol at which they will phosphorylate (Sasaki et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sasaki et al., 2009.

claim: Many proteins contain domains that bind PI3P (PX and FYVE) and PI4P (FAPP and OSBP).
source: For example, many proteins contain domains that bind PI3P (PX and FYVE) and PI4P (FAPP and OSBP) and numerous PH domains that bind various PIs with differing degrees of affinity and selectivity have been reported (Hammond and Balla, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hammond and Balla, 2015.

claim: A recent biochemical study has identified a large number of proteins that bind a range of PIs with varying degrees of specificity.
source: Indeed, a recent biochemical study has identified a large number of proteins that bind a range of PIs with varying degrees of specificity (Jungmichel et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jungmichel et al., 2014.

claim: A detailed annotation of the PI signaling genes in the Drosophila genome led to the identification of 103 genes which are part of the PI signaling toolkit.
source: A detailed annotation of the PI signaling genes in the Drosophila genome (Balakrishnan et al., 2015) led to the identification of 103 genes which are part of the PI signaling toolkit (Figure 1) and conserved between flies and other organisms important for the study of developmental processes and disease biology.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Balakrishnan et al., 2015 and is the basis for the study.

claim: The 103 PI signaling genes are conserved between flies and other organisms important for the study of developmental processes and disease biology.
source: A detailed annotation of the PI signaling genes in the Drosophila genome (Balakrishnan et al., 2015) led to the identification of 103 genes which are part of the PI signaling toolkit (Figure 1) and conserved between flies and other organisms important for the study of developmental processes and disease biology.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Balakrishnan et al., 2015.

claim: The GAL4/UAS system allows for tight spatial and temporal gene modulation in Drosophila.
source: Further the availability of binary gene expression control systems such as the GAL4/UAS system allow for tight spatial and temporal gene modulation in turn allowing sophisticated analysis of both cell autonomous and non-cell autonomous modes of developmental control by PI signaling (Colombani et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Colombani et al., 2005.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 has emerged as a powerful tool for genome editing in multiple organisms including flies.
source: In the recent years, CRISPR/Cas9 has emerged as a powerful tool for genome editing in multiple organisms including flies (Gratz et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gratz et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2018.

claim: Transgenic fly lines expressing RNAi constructs are available against almost the entire fly genome.
source: However, unlike transgenic fly lines expressing RNAi constructs that are available against almost the entire fly genome (Dietzl et al., 2007; Perkins et al., 2015), efforts to make guide RNA (gRNA) expressing transgenic flies are still underway (Meltzer et al., 2019; Port et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dietzl et al., 2007 and Perkins et al., 2015.

claim: A genome editing system was generated that can be used for Cas9 mediated editing to delete the open-reading frame of each of the 103 annotated PI signaling genes.
source: In this study, we have generated a genome editing system that can be used for Cas9 mediated editing to delete the open-reading frame of each of the 103 annotated genes that could regulate PI signaling (Balakrishnan et al., 2015; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is the main contribution of the study, demonstrated throughout the Results section.

claim: The guides were used to generate both whole body knock outs as well as tissue specific, developmentally timed depletion of individual genes with high efficiency.
source: Importantly, we use these guides to generate both whole body knock outs as well as tissue specific, developmentally timed depletion of individual genes with high efficiency.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the Results section with experimental data.

claim: A genetic screen in the developing Drosophila eye identified key roles for PI signaling.
source: Further, using these reagents we present the results of a genetic screen in the developing Drosophila eye and identify key roles for PI signaling in this influential model of tissue development and patterning.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the Results section with experimental data and images.

claim: A single mismatch in the target sequence may highly reduce the efficiency of CRISPR.
source: Firstly, CRISPR-Cas9-based genome editing is highly robust and specific; a single mismatch in the target sequence may highly reduce the efficiency of CRISPR (Pattanayak et al., 2013), especially if the mismatches are present in the core 12 bp protospacer region most proximal to the protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) site.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pattanayak et al., 2013.

claim: The entire genome of S2R+ cells and the isogenized attP40 parent fly stock were sequenced.
source: The entire genome of S2R+ cells as well as the isogenized attP40 parent fly stock (BDSC 25709: y1 v1 P{y[+t7.7]=nos-phiC31\int.NLS}X; P{y[+t7.7]=CaryP}attP40) that was to be used to generate dgRNA transgenic flies were sequenced (sequencing data is available for S2R+ cells on hyperlink and for isogenized attP40 stock on hyperlink).
evidence: This is a methodological step described in the study.

claim: Both the isogenized parent fly stock and the S2R+ cell genome sequences showed more than 600,000 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) when aligned against the reference genome.
source: When aligned against the reference genome, both the isogenized parent fly stock and the S2R+ cell genome sequences showed more than 600,000 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) (Supplementary file 3, 4).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Supplementary files 3 and 4.

claim: The genome sequences had ~1.3 million mismatches (SNP, insertions, and deletions) when compared to each other.
source: When compared to each other, these genome sequences had ~1.3 million mismatches (SNP, insertions, and deletions) suggesting that, as expected, almost all the sequence differences in the two genomes were independent of each other (Supplementary file 3, 4).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Supplementary files 3 and 4.

claim: Only 1 gRNA target (targeting CG10426), out of the 206 generated, seemed to have one base mismatch.
source: Only 1 gRNA target (targeting CG10426), out of the 206 generated, seemed to have one base mismatch marked in red (Supplementary file 1), while the other 205 targets matched between all the genomes.
evidence: This is supported by data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: For each gene, two regions were identified wherein an sgRNA would be designed to target each region.
source: For each gene, two regions were identified wherein an sgRNA would be designed to target each region. The first sgRNA would be designed to target the first coding exon and the second sgRNA to target the exon with the stop codon (Figure 2).
evidence: This is the design strategy described in the Methods and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: The OCRL polypeptide of the expected Mr of ca. 100 kDa is completely absent in ocrlKO lysates.
source: The OCRL polypeptide of the expected Mr of ca. 100 kDa is completely absent in ocrlKO lysates.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B by western blot analysis.

claim: The OCRL protein is seen in punctate structures throughout the cell body in wild-type nephrocytes.
source: As expected, the OCRL protein (magenta) is seen in punctate structures throughout the cell body. This staining is completely absent in ocrlKO animals.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C by immunolabeling.

claim: OCRL staining is completely absent in ocrlKO animals.
source: As expected, the OCRL protein (magenta) is seen in punctate structures throughout the cell body. This staining is completely absent in ocrlKO animals.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C by immunolabeling.

claim: The 555 bp diagnostic band is seen in the ocrl KO and nephrocyte-specific knockout DNA but not in wild-type flies.
source: The 555 bp diagnostic band is seen in the ocrl KO and nephrocyte-specific knockout DNA but not in wild-type flies and in NTC (no template control).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D by PCR analysis.

claim: There is no detectable signal for OCRL in the nephrocytes of nephrocyte specific knockout animals.
source: There is no detectable signal for OCRL in the nephrocytes of nephrocyte specific knockout animals; the experiment was repeated twice and 24 individual nephrocytes images from multiple animals.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E by immunostaining.

claim: The expected molecular size of Cas9 is 158 kD.
source: The expected molecular size of Cas9 is 158 kD (the band of highest intensity indicated with a '*').
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B by western blot analysis.

claim: The Cas9 antibody cross-reacts with a protein from S2R+ cells.
source: Note that the Cas9 antibody cross-reacts with a protein from S2R+ cells ('#') thereby precluding immunocytochemical detection of Cas9 in S2R+ cells.
evidence: This is noted in Figure 3B.

claim: The presence of a 358 bp band in cells expressing Cas9 compared to the 1739 bp band in untransfected cells suggests the successful deletion of CG5734.
source: The presence of a 358 bp band in cells expressing Cas9 compared to the 1739 bp band in untransfected cells suggests the successful deletion of CG5734.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C by genomic PCR.

claim: Cas9 was predominantly localized in the nucleus suggesting efficient nuclear localization by the NLS.
source: Cas9 (grayscale) was predominantly localized in the nucleus suggesting efficient nuclear localization by the NLS.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D by immunostaining of salivary glands.

claim: Expected genomic deletions were identified in DNA obtained from fly heads but not in DNA obtained from the fly body suggesting tissue (eye)-specific gene deletion.
source: Expected genomic deletions were identified in DNA obtained from fly heads but not in DNA obtained from the fly body suggesting tissue (eye)-specific gene deletion using our newly generated reagents (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A by genomic PCR.

claim: Deletion of Class I PI3K (Dp110) resulted in smaller eyes compared to controls.
source: Deletion of Class I PI3K (Dp110), that converts PI(4,5)P2 to PI(3,4,5)P3 resulted in smaller eyes compared to controls.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and Figure 5.

claim: The role of PI3K in cell growth is in agreement with a number of studies.
source: This is in agreement with a number of studies that have established the importance of PI3K for cell growth (Goberdhan et al., 1999; Weinkove et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Goberdhan et al., 1999 and Weinkove et al., 1999.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of Dp110 resulted in ~40% reduction in eye size compared to controls.
source: While the RNAi-mediated knockdown resulted in ~40% reduction [Figure 5A (ii) and (iii) and C] compared to controls [Figure 5A (i)], dgRNA mediated Dp110 knockout showed a stronger phenotype with eyes ~ 75% smaller [Figure 5B (ii) and C] than appropriate controls [Figure 5B (i)] thus demonstrating that these dgRNAs serve as efficient tools to study tissue-specific roles of genes.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A and quantified in Figure 5C.

claim: dgRNA mediated Dp110 knockout showed a stronger phenotype with eyes ~ 75% smaller than appropriate controls.
source: While the RNAi-mediated knockdown resulted in ~40% reduction [Figure 5A (ii) and (iii) and C] compared to controls [Figure 5A (i)], dgRNA mediated Dp110 knockout showed a stronger phenotype with eyes ~ 75% smaller [Figure 5B (ii) and C] than appropriate controls [Figure 5B (i)] thus demonstrating that these dgRNAs serve as efficient tools to study tissue-specific roles of genes.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B and quantified in Figure 5C.

claim: CRISPR-mediated Pten deletion results in eyes larger than control eyes.
source: CRISPR-mediated Pten deletion results in eyes larger than control eyes.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B(iii) and quantified in Figure 5C.

claim: When both Dp110 and Pten are targeted simultaneously, the size of the eyes are intermediate between the small eyes seen with Dp110 deletion and the large eyes seen with Pten deletion.
source: When both Dp110 and Pten are targeted simultaneously, the size of the eyes are intermediate between the small eyes seen with Dp110 deletion and the large eyes seen with Pten deletion.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B(iv) and quantified in Figure 5C.

claim: Class I PI3K (encoded by Dp110) phosphorylates PIP2 to generate PIP3.
source: Class I PI3K (encoded by Dp110) phosphorylates PIP2 to generate PIP3 while the lipid phosphatase PTEN (encoded by Pten) dephosphorylates PIP3 to generate PIP2.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about PI metabolism.

claim: The lipid phosphatase PTEN (encoded by Pten) dephosphorylates PIP3 to generate PIP2.
source: Class I PI3K (encoded by Dp110) phosphorylates PIP2 to generate PIP3 while the lipid phosphatase PTEN (encoded by Pten) dephosphorylates PIP3 to generate PIP2.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about PI metabolism.

claim: Disruption of Pten was able to rescue the phenotype of the disruption of Dp110 and vice versa.
source: Disruption of Pten was able to rescue the phenotype of the disruption of Dp110 and vice versa.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B(iv) and quantified in Figure 5C.

claim: RDGB (retinal degeneration B) is a PI transfer protein, depletion of which leads to light-dependent phototransduction defects.
source: RDGB (retinal degeneration B) is a PI transfer protein (encoded by rdgB), depletion of which leads to light-dependent phototransduction defects (Yadav et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yadav et al., 2015.

claim: Whole body mutants of rdgB are viable with no morphological defects in the eye.
source: Whole body mutants of rdgB are viable with no morphological defects in the eye (Yadav et al., 2015), although electrical recordings (ERG) from the eye of rdgB mutants show reduced amplitude.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yadav et al., 2015.

claim: Electrical recordings (ERG) from the eye of rdgB mutants show reduced amplitude.
source: Whole body mutants of rdgB are viable with no morphological defects in the eye (Yadav et al., 2015), although electrical recordings (ERG) from the eye of rdgB mutants show reduced amplitude.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yadav et al., 2015.

claim: ERG recordings from the germline knockout of rdgB generated using CRISPR/Cas9 was comparable to rdgB2.
source: ERG recordings from this germline knockout of rdgB generated using CRISPR/Cas9 was comparable to rdgB2 (Figure 6B), an amorphic allele generated by chemical mutagenesis in the Benzer lab (Harris and Stark, 1977).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B and supported by citation to Harris and Stark, 1977.

claim: Germline knockouts of 48 genes were generated using the dgRNA transgenic flies.
source: In a similar manner, using the dgRNA transgenic flies, we generated germline knockouts of several additional genes (total 48 genes) by crossing them to either nanos, vasa or Act5c-Cas9 flies (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is documented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The deletions obtained are highly efficient between 4 and 100% efficiency in F1 flies and between 3–70% efficiency in F2 flies.
source: The deletions obtained in this manner are highly efficient between 4 and 100% efficiency in F1 flies and between 3–70% efficiency in F2 flies (absolute values provided in Supplementary file 1) in generating germline knockouts with deletions ranging in size between 400 bp and 38 kb.
evidence: This is documented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Germline knockouts have deletions ranging in size between 400 bp and 38 kb.
source: The deletions obtained in this manner are highly efficient between 4 and 100% efficiency in F1 flies and between 3–70% efficiency in F2 flies (absolute values provided in Supplementary file 1) in generating germline knockouts with deletions ranging in size between 400 bp and 38 kb.
evidence: This is documented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: For 13 genes, germline deletions could not be generated despite repeated attempts.
source: For a few genes (13 genes), we were unable to generate germline deletions despite repeated attempts in some cases possibly due to their essential roles in gametogenesis or embryogenesis.
evidence: This is a negative result reported in the study.

claim: Western blot analysis showed that eye-specific Cas9 expression was not sufficient to knockout rdgB and detectable levels of RDGB protein was still present.
source: Western blot analysis showed that eye-specific Cas9 expression was not sufficient to knockout rdgB and detectable levels of RDGB protein was still present.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A by western blot.

claim: The mean amplitude from ERG recordings of eye-specific rdgB deletion flies was the same as control flies.
source: The mean amplitude from ERG recordings of these flies was the same as control flies.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Western blot analysis of whole fly rdgB deletion showed a complete loss of RDGB similar to the rdgB2 null mutant flies.
source: The same dgRNA flies were used to generate a whole fly rdgB deletion (rdgBCRISPR KO) and western blot analysis showed a complete loss of RDGB similar to the rdgB2 null mutant flies.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C by western blot.

claim: Both rdgB2 and rdgBCRISPR KO flies showed complete loss of ERG amplitudes.
source: Both rdgB2 and rdgBCRISPR KO flies showed complete loss of ERG amplitudes as expected.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D.

claim: skittles (sktl) is a PI4P 5-kinase known to have a role during larval development.
source: skittles (sktl) is a PI4P 5-kinase known to have a role during larval development (Hassan et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hassan et al., 1998.

claim: Mutations in sktl are organismal lethal as well as cell lethal.
source: Mutations in sktl are organismal lethal as well as cell lethal.
evidence: This is established knowledge about sktl.

claim: Out of the 141 F2 flies sequenced for sktl, 132 showed in-frame indels with an intact kinase domain, with the largest deletion being 24 bp.
source: Out of the 141 F2 flies sequenced, 132 showed in-frame indels with an intact kinase domain, with the largest deletion being 24 bp.
evidence: This is sequencing data from the study.

claim: The sktl sgRNA were highly efficient at targeting sktl but only cells with at least a partially functional protein managed to survive during eye development.
source: This suggests that the sktl sgRNA were highly efficient at targeting sktl but only cells with at least a partially functional protein managed to survive during eye development and therefore appeared morphologically normal.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sequencing data and phenotypic observations.

claim: The study uncovered the function of 30 PI signaling genes in eye development.
source: Using this method, we uncovered the function of 30 PI signaling genes in eye development and nine genes previously not implicated in this process.
evidence: This is a summary of the screen results.

claim: Nine genes previously not implicated in eye development were identified.
source: Using this method, we uncovered the function of 30 PI signaling genes in eye development and nine genes previously not implicated in this process.
evidence: This is a summary of the screen results.

claim: The toolkit includes reagents for editing ca. 72 PI binding proteins.
source: However, the tool kit presented here includes reagents for editing ca. 72 PI binding proteins.
evidence: This is based on the composition of the 103 gene toolkit.

claim: The UAS-Cas9-T2A-eGFP construct provides the advantage that all cells expressing Cas9 also express eGFP.
source: The system we have developed includes a number of innovative features. In the study of cell-cell interactions in development, it is desirable and indeed essential to mark the cell types in which gene manipulation is being performed. To facilitate this, we have designed an UAS-Cas9-T2A-eGFP construct which provides many advantages: (i) All cells expressing Cas9 also express eGFP thus marking cells guaranteed to express Cas9.
evidence: This is a design feature of the construct described in the study.

claim: Since Cas9 and eGFP are expressed as independent proteins, the possibility of a Cas9 fusion protein with reduced function is eliminated.
source: (ii) Since Cas9 and eGFP are expressed as independent proteins, the possibility of a Cas9 fusion protein with reduced function is eliminated.
evidence: This is a design feature of the construct described in the study.

claim: The UAS-Cas9-T2A-eGFP avoids the need for two independent genetic elements to express both Cas9 and eGFP.
source: (iii) The UAS-Cas9-T2A-eGFP presented here avoids the need for two independent genetic elements to express both Cas9 and eGFP thus reducing the complexity of strain construction.
evidence: This is a design feature of the construct described in the study.

claim: The use of Cas9 with an NLS ensures that the protein is nuclear localized maximizing the probability of gene editing activity.
source: (iv) The use of Cas9 with an NLS ensures that the protein is nuclear localized maximizing the probability of gene editing activity.
evidence: This is a design feature of the construct described in the study.

claim: Cas9 can be expressed in a mosaic fashion under the control of the Gal4/UAS system using the CoinFLP method.
source: For example, in addition to the basic eye development screen presented here as an illustrative example, Cas9 can be expressed in a mosaic fashion under the control of the Gal4/UAS system using the CoinFLP method (Bosch et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bosch et al., 2015.

claim: A recent study has presented evidence of a role of some genes involved in PI signaling as regulators of cell competition during eye development.
source: Indeed, a recent study has presented evidence of a role of some genes involved in PI signaling as regulators of cell competition during eye development (Janardan et al., 2020) and the expanded repertoire of editing reagents generated during this study will allow the mechanism by which PI signaling regulates cell competition to be analysed in greater detail.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Janardan et al., 2020.

claim: Recent studies have used the approach of having two sgRNAs both targeting the coding region immediately downstream of the start codon.
source: Recent studies have used the approach of having two sgRNAs both targeting the coding region immediately downstream of the start codon with the expectation of maximizing the likelihood of a frameshift mutation to achieve loss of function (Port et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Port et al., 2020.

claim: The dgRNA containing transgenic flies target both the first and the last exon and result in complete deletion of the gene.
source: Secondly, because our dgRNA containing transgenic flies target both the first and the last exon and result in complete deletion of the gene, the subsequent introduction of a copy of the gene with homologous arms (Baena-Lopez et al., 2013) would result in gene knock-ins and reconstitution of function.
evidence: This is a design feature of the approach described in the study, with citation to Baena-Lopez et al., 2013.

claim: In the case of the PI4P 5-kinase sktl, eye-specific deletion resulted in morphologically normal looking eyes because cells lacking sktl were eliminated early in eye disc development.
source: For example, in the case of the PI4P 5-kinase sktl, eye-specific deletion resulted in morphologically normal looking eyes. The reason for this was most likely that cells lacking sktl were eliminated (due to the essential nature of the gene product) early in eye disc development and only those cells with indels that are multiples of three bases thus possibly producing a partially functional protein survived.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations and sequencing data.

claim: The residual protein in eye-specific editing of rdgB most likely results from the long half-life of the protein that was present from early development.
source: We therefore speculate that the residual protein in eye-specific editing of rdgB most likely results from the long half-life of the protein that was present from early development.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental observations.

claim: The lack of a phenotype in tissue-specific gene disruptions using dgRNA will not be conclusive.
source: Therefore, absence of phenotypes in these tissue-specific gene disruptions using dgRNA will not be conclusive and under these circumstances, generation of a germline knock out would be valuable.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the limitations observed in the study.

claim: Out of 103 genes, 102 gave the desired deletion product when crossed to Act5c-Cas9 flies.
source: Once generated, all the dgRNA transgenics were crossed to Act5c-Cas9 (BDSC 54590: y1 M{Act5C-Cas9.P}ZH-2A w*) flies and larval progeny were tested for deletions by PCR and sequencing. Out of 103 genes, 102 gave the desired deletion product, while one did not give a band of the expected length (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from testing the dgRNA lines.

claim: One dgRNA did not give a band of the expected length when crossed to Act5c-Cas9 flies.
source: Out of 103 genes, 102 gave the desired deletion product, while one did not give a band of the expected length (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from testing the dgRNA lines.

claim: Deletion of Pten resulted in a wing blade larger than that of controls.
